name: Sedge meadow and the wet toe of the banks
reads_as: dense sedge that hides everything in it — rails calling from three feet away and never seen, voles under the thatch, and mosquitoes

soundscape.note: The defining fact of this zone is that its animals are AUDIBLE AND NOT VISIBLE. Rails, bitterns and voles are all present at densities a walker would never guess from what can be seen, which is the case liberty L2 was written for.

status.note: Named in the regional wet-prairie assemblage the dossier quotes from an Illinois DNR wetlands publication; The dossier's citation for this has no record in data/sources/, so nothing here is graded documented on it.

presence.note: The most conspicuous bird in any Illinois marsh or sedge meadow.

abundance.note: By July the territorial males are joined by fledged young and the birds start to gather — this is the one bird of the July list that is genuinely numerous.

july.behaviour: Males on sedge tussocks and cattail stems, spreading red epaulets; birds mobbing a passing harrier or crow.
july.appearance: Glossy black male with red-and-buff shoulder; streaky brown female low in the sedge.

species.note: Song is declining by 1 July as the second broods fledge — the konk-la-ree is still there but the wall of it belongs to May.

status.note: A wet-meadow and marsh-edge breeder in the dossier's oak-savanna and marsh-edge list; regional inference.

presence.note: Sings from cover and is rarely in the open.

july.behaviour: Sound only in most conditions: a rolling witchety-witchety-witchety from deep in the sedge, moving as the bird moves.
july.appearance: Small olive warbler; the male's black mask is visible only at very close range.

species.note: One of the small set of warblers still in strong song on 1 July — yellowthroats are double-brooded and sing on through the month, so full song here is a July fact rather than a spring holdover.

status.note: Rails are named in the regional wet-prairie assemblage; The dossier's citation for this has no record in data/sources/, so nothing here is graded documented on it.

presence.note: A textbook 'present but never seen' bird: heard from ten feet away and invisible.

abundance.note: Habitat reading; density in dense sedge is unknowable by eye.

july.behaviour: Sound only: a descending whinny and a sharp rising ker-wee from inside the sedge, answered from a second point, with nothing visible at either.

species.note: Nothing is drawn for this species anywhere in the dataset. It is present as sound only, which is the case liberty L2 exists to license.

status.note: As for sora; the same regional assemblage.

presence.note: Invisible in cover; identified only by voice.

july.behaviour: Sound only: a hard descending grunt series and a metallic kid-ick from the wettest sedge.

species.note: Rails are named only at the level of the regional wet-prairie assemblage, from a source with no record in data/sources/. Nothing puts this species at Chicago in 1835; the habitat does.

status.note: Regional retrospective; The dossier's citation for this has no record in data/sources/, so nothing here is graded documented on it.

presence.note: Sign only, as on the open prairie.

abundance.note: Sedge meadow is prime vole ground.

july.behaviour: Nothing animate; runways and clippings only.
july.trace: Runways through the sedge thatch and clipped stem piles at the tussock bases.

species.note: 'Meadow/prairie mouse' in the regional retrospective is as close as the record gets. The species reading and the density are both this project's.

status.note: Garter snakes are in the regional herp list the dossier quotes; The dossier's citation for this has no record in data/sources/, so nothing here is graded documented on it. The dossier calls garter and water snakes the plausible town-edge species.

presence.note: Basking on a bare verge or crossing a trail in the morning.

july.behaviour: A single snake stretched on a warm bare verge in the morning, moving off into the sedge.

species.note: The regional herp list names garter snakes without a date or a place; the dossier calls garter and water snakes the plausible town-edge species and tags that inference, as this record does.

status.note: Damp meadow is the species' core habitat.

presence.note: The dusk display, and only at dusk.

abundance.note: Wet ground and long grass together are the ideal case.

july.behaviour: Dense flashing low over the sedge in the half hour after sunset; the J-shaped upsweep about every five or six seconds.

species.note: The species, the month and the city are all in modern natural-history sources; 1835 is the inference, and it runs the safe way — the pre-drainage landscape would have supported more fireflies than the modern one, not fewer.

presence.note: Continuous fine ticking; nothing to draw.

abundance.note: Sedge meadow is where this group is densest.

july.behaviour: Sound only: a fine, high, continuous shimmer over the whole meadow, day and night.

species.note: Genus-level: the dossier names meadow katydids as a group and no species-level Chicago record exists for any date.

status.note: The dossier's Chicago 1834 description — residents 'situated in the midst of sloughs and marshes and the sluggish Chicago River', in log buildings without screens, the slough producing 'clouds of mosquitoes carrying the ague' — comes from a page that returned HTTP 403 to the research agent, so the exact wording is unverified and The dossier's citation for this has no record in data/sources/, so nothing here is graded documented on it.

presence.note: Individual mosquitoes will not read at any render scale. They are recorded as present and maximal, and the correct rendering of them is the human response — smudge fires, netting, covered arms — which liberty L1 puts out of scope for v1. So this zone's single most intense July fact is deliberately shown as nothing.

abundance.note: Maximal. Standing water, no drainage, no screens, and endemic ague.

july.behaviour: Nothing is drawn. A smudge-fire smoke plume is the only defensible visible trace, and that belongs to the structures dataset, not to this one.

species.note: Recorded because leaving the defining insect of a July Chicago wetland out of the dataset would misrepresent the place far more than rendering nothing for it does.

note: The species list is the regional wet-prairie assemblage the dossier quotes from an Illinois DNR wetlands publication, which has no source record in data/sources/. Nothing in this zone is attested at Chicago in 1835 and nothing in it is graded documented.
